SUBJECT:      PALISADES NUCLEAR PLANT – NRC INITIAL LICENSE EXAMINATION
              REPORT 05000255/2026301

Dear Michael Schultheis:

On August 17, 2026, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) completed the initial
operator licensing examination process for license applicants employed at your Palisades
Nuclear Plant. The enclosed report documents the results of those examinations. Preliminary
observations noted during the examination process were discussed on August 3, 2026, with
Derek DeBusscher and other members of your staff. An exit meeting was conducted via
Microsoft Teams on September 3, 2026, between yourself and James Nance Senior Operations
Engineer, to review the proposed final grading of the written examination for the license
applicants. During the exit meeting, the NRC resolutions of any post-examination comments
submitted by the facility, initially received by the NRC on August 17, 2026, were discussed.

The NRC examiners administered an initial license examination operating test during the week
of July 27, 2026. The written examination was administered by Palisades Nuclear Plant training
department personnel on August 5, 2026. Nine Senior Reactor Operator and six Reactor
Operator applicants were administered license examinations. The results of the examinations
were finalized on August 31, 2026. Six applicants passed all sections of their respective
examinations. Nine applicants were issued Preliminary Results letters. Three were issued
senior operator licenses and three were issued operator licenses.

The as-administered written examination and operating test, as well as documents related to the
development and review (outlines, review comments and resolution, etc.) of the examination will
be withheld from public disclosure until August 17, 2028. Hower, since nine applicants received
a Preliminary Results letter because of a written examination grade that was less than
80 percent overall or less than 70 percent for the SRO Only portion of their exam, the applicants
were provided copies of the written examination. For examination security purposes, your staff
should consider that written examination uncontrolled and exposed to the public.
 M. Schultheis                                 2


This letter, its enclosure, and your response (if any) will be made available for public inspection
and copying at http://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/adams.html and at the NRC Public Document

Inspections, Exemptions, Requests for Withholding.”

                                    SUMMARY OF FINDINGS

ER 05000255/2026301; 7/27/2026-8/17/2026; Palisades Energy, LLC, Palisades Nuclear Plant.
Initial License Examination Report.

The announced initial operator licensing examination was conducted by regional Nuclear
Regulatory Commission (NRC) examiners in accordance with the guidance of NUREG-1021,
“Operator Licensing Examination Standards for Power Reactors,” Revision 12.

Examination Summary:

Six of fifteen applicants passed all sections of their respective examinations. Three applicants
were issued senior operator licenses and three applicants were issued operator licenses.
Nine applicants were issued Preliminary Results letters for failure of one or more sections of
the administered examination. (Section 4OA5.1).




                                                2
                                         REPORT DETAILS

4OA5 Other Activities

 .1    Initial Licensing Examinations

  a.   Examination Scope

       The NRC examiners and members of the facility licensee’s staff used the guidance
       prescribed in NUREG-1021, “Operator Licensing Examination Standards for Power
       Reactors,” Revision 12, to develop, validate, administer, and grade the written
       examination and operating test. The written examination outlines were prepared by
       the NRC staff and were transmitted to the facility licensee’s staff. Members of the facility
       licensee’s staff developed the operating test outlines and developed the written
       examination and operating test. The NRC examiners validated the proposed
       examination during the week of June 22, 2026, with the assistance of members of the
       facility licensee’s staff. During the on-site validation week, the examiners audited all
       license applications for accuracy. The NRC examiners administered the operating test,
       consisting of job performance measures and dynamic simulator scenarios, during the
       period of July 27, 2026 through July 31, 2026. The facility licensee administered the
       written examination on August 5, 2026.

       On August 17, 2026, the licensee submitted documentation noting that there were five
       post-examination comments for consideration by the NRC examiners when grading the
       written examination. The post-examination comments and the NRC resolution for the
       post-examination comments are provided in Enclosure 2 to this report.

  b.   Findings

  (1) Written Examination

       The NRC examiners determined that the written examination, as proposed by the
       licensee, was within the range of acceptability expected for a proposed examination.
       Less than 20 percent of the proposed examination questions were determined to be
       unsatisfactory and required modification or replacement.

       During validation of the written examination, several questions were modified or
       replaced. All changes made to the proposed written examination, were made in
       accordance with NUREG-1021, “Operator Licensing Examination Standards for Power
       Reactors,” and documented on Form 2.3-5, “Written Examination Review Worksheet.”
       The Form 2.3-5, the written examination outlines, and both the proposed and final
       written examinations, will be available electronically in the NRC Public Document Room
       or from the Publicly Available Records component of NRC’s Agencywide Documents
       Access and Management System (ADAMS) on August 17, 2028, (ADAMS Accession
       Numbers administrative files ML25156A224, examination outlines ML25156A226,
       proposed exam ML25156A227, and as-administered exam ML25156A223.

       The NRC examiners graded the written examination on August 26, 2026, and
       conducted a review of each missed question to determine the accuracy and validity
       of the examination questions. There were five questions associated with operator
       actions in response to abnormal and emergency events, five questions associated
       with plant systems, and two questions associated with generic nuclear topics where


                                                3
       post-examination analysis identified generic weaknesses in that more than 50 percent
      of the applicants responded incorrectly to these questions.

 (2) Operating Test

      The NRC examiners determined that the operating test, as originally proposed by the
      licensee, was within the range of acceptability expected for a proposed examination.
      Less than 20 percent of the proposed operating test portion of the examination was
      determined to be unsatisfactory and required modification or replacement.

      During the validation of the operating test, several Job Performance Measures (JPMs)
      were modified or replaced, and some modifications were made to the dynamic simulator
      scenarios. Changes made to the operating test portion of the examination, were made
      in accordance with NUREG-1021, “Operator Licensing Examination Standards for
      Power Reactors,” and documented on Form 2.3-3, “Operating Test Review Worksheet.”
      The Form 2.3-3, the operating test outlines, and both the proposed and final as
      administered dynamic simulator scenarios and JPMs, will be available electronically
      in the NRC Public Document Room or from the Publicly Available Records component of
      NRC's ADAMS on August 17, 2028, (ADAMS Accession Numbers administrative files
      ML25156A224, examination outlines ML25156A226, proposed exam ML25156A227,
      and as-administered exam ML25156A223).

      The NRC examiners completed operating test grading on August 31, 2026.
      Post-examination analysis revealed generic weaknesses in locating certain in-plant
      components and determining the appropriate Technical Specifications and which
      Limiting Conditions for Operations (LCOs) to enter into during scenarios and while
      performing certain Administrative Job Performance Measures (JPMs).

 (3) Examination Results

      Nine SRO and six RO applicants were administered examinations. Three SRO
      applicants were issued senior operator licenses, and three RO applicants were issued
      operator licenses.

.2    Examination Security

 a.   Scope

      The NRC examiners reviewed and observed the licensee's implementation of
      examination security requirements during the examination validation and administration
      to assure compliance with Title10 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Section 55.49,
      “Integrity of Examinations and Tests.” The examiners used the guidelines provided in
      NUREG 1021, "Operator Licensing Examination Standards for Power Reactors,” to
      determine acceptability of the licensee’s examination security activities.

 b.   Findings

      None.




                                             4
 4OA6 Meetings

 .1   Debrief

      The chief examiner presented the examination team's preliminary observations and
      findings on August 3, 2026, to Derek DeBusscher, Assistant Operations Manager – Shift
      and other members of the Palisades Nuclear Plant Operations and Training Department
      staff.

 .2   Exit Meeting

      The chief examiner conducted an exit meeting on September 3, 2026, with Michael
      Schultheis, Site Vice President via Microsoft Teams. The NRC’s final disposition of
      the station’s grading of the written examination and post-examination comments were
      disclosed and discussed during the exit meeting. The chief examiner asked the licensee
      whether any of the retained submitted material used to develop or administer the
      examination should be considered proprietary. No proprietary or sensitive information
      was identified during the examination or debrief/exit meetings.

Question #5

   •   The Unit is at 100% power
   •   Single Charging and Letdown is in service
   •   P-55A, Charging Pump, is running

Subsequently

   •   The CCW line to P-55A develops a leak
   •   P-55A trips

P-55A tripped due to high ___(1)___ temperature.
Per AOP-22 (PRESSURIZER LEVEL CONTROL MALFUNCTIONS), the letdown orifice stop
valves (HS-2003, 2004, & 2005) ___(2)___ closed prior to starting another Charing Pump.

                        (1)           (2)
       A.            motor            are
       B.            motor          are NOT
       C.            fluid drive      are
       D.            fluid drive    are NOT


Answer: D

   A. Incorrect but plausible. For Part 1, CCW does not cool the CCP motors. It is plausible
      because it does cool the pump oil coolers. For Part 2, AOP-22 Step 8.d RNO requires
      the letdown orifice to be closed if the charging pump is in distress.

   B. Incorrect but plausible. For Part 1, CCW does not cool the CCP motors. It is plausible
      because it does cool the pump oil coolers. Part 2 is correct.

   C. Incorrect but plausible. Part 1 is correct. For Part 2, AOP-22 Step 8.d RNO requires the
      letdown orifice to be closed if the charging pump is in distress.

   D. CORRECT. For Part 1, CCW cools the pump lube oil coolers / fluid drive. At 150oF fluid
      drive temperature, the CCP trips. For Part 2 and per AOP-22 Step 8, the letdown orifice
      isolation valve is NOT closed prior to starting another Charging Pump.




                                                                                   Enclosure 2
 Question Development:

During examination outline development, Question 5 was selected as Knowledge and Ability
(K/A) 000022A AK2.07, to be a Tier 1 question. Questions formulated from this tier are generally
expected to test an applicant’s knowledge of how to safely operate the plant during emergency
and abnormal conditions.

Question 5 was developed by Palisades for use on the 2026 Palisades Initial License Written
Examination. There were no technical or psychometric errors identified by the NRC examination
review team or the Palisades Training Department staff regarding this question during
examination review and facility validation.

Knowledge and Ability (K/A) Statement: Knowledge of the relationship between (APE 22) LOSS
OF REACTOR COOLANT MAKEUP and the following systems or components (CFR: 41.7 /
45.7): CCWS Rating 3.2

Question Administration:

NUREG-1021, ES-4.3, item B.2.i, identifies that for applicants taking the RO written
examination, six hours is to be allotted.

   •   One applicant asked a question during the examination regarding the letdown orifice
       isolation valve equipment part numbers. This information was provided to all applicants
       during the examination
   •   Seven (of fifteen) applicants correctly answered this question. All other applicants
       selected choice C. (46.6% pass rate)
   •   The question was originally assessed as an enhancement by the NRC Chief Examiner
       during review of the proposed exam due to recommended items to be added to the
       distractor analysis.
   •   A post-examination comment proposed an answer key change for Question 5.
       The facility/applicants contesting the question believe there are two correct answers
       for Question 5, answers C and D.

Facility/Applicant Comment:

Per AOP-22, P55A charging pump tripped on high fluid drive temperature. Step 8.b states,
“verify charging pumps not in distress.” With a lowering CCW and P-55A tripping charging
pumps indicate in distress. Therefore, all pumps are tripped, and letdown is isolated prior to
starting charging pumps.

Question 5 has two technically correct answers. Palisades’ position is that both Answer C and
Answer D are correct.

Per NUREG 1021, ES 4.4, C.3.c, the question stem was not clear or did not contain all pertinent
information to distinguish between two answer choices.




                                                2
 Facility/Applicant Justification for Comment:

For Part 2 of the question, either answer choices C and D can be justified based on the
procedural guidance provided. Given P-55A is identified as tripped due to high fluid drive
temperature in the stem of the question, a candidate could reasonably conclude that the pump
is in distress. Following AOP-22, Step 8.b directs the operator to proceed to Step 8.b.1 (RNO),
which then directs entry into Step 8.d.1, where the operator is instructed to close the letdown
orifice isolation valves in Step 8.d.4. Therefore, the letdown flow path would be isolated via the
letdown orifice stop valves prior to starting a charging pump. A candidate adhering to the
procedure as written could reasonably select the answer corresponding to closing the valves
before starting a charging pump.

However, given that P-55A tripped due to a high fluid drive temperature, a protective feature,
a candidate can reasonably determine the pump was not in distress. Therefore, Step 8.b
(“VERIFY charging pump(s) are NOT in distress (e.g., rattles and bangs indicative of pumping
non-liquid fluids)”) would be answered YES, subsequently directing starting available charging
pumps in Step 8.c without first closing the letdown orifice stop valves.

Based on the lack of information provided in the question stem to discern whether or not the
charging pump was truly in distress or not, and per AOP-22 procedural guidance, both answers
C and D are technically supportable and should be considered correct.

NRC Assessment:

The question stem addresses a CCW leak on the cooling line specific to charging pump P-55A.
The applicant in their contention makes an assumption regarding the status of the CCW.
Specifically, the applicant assumes the level in the CCW surge tank is lowering and cannot be
recovered. There is no discussion as to whether the automatic makeup for CCW would account
for this leak or whether operator actions which would be performed per AOP-36, Loss of
Component Cooling would have been effective. Since level in the CCW surge tank would
initially lower and the question stem indicated that a CCW cooled component (P-55A) had
degraded cooling, the entry criteria of AOP-36 have been met and the actions of that procedure
would be expected to be performed. Step 2 of AOP-36 has the crew check if CCW surge tank
level is rising or stable. Based on the discussion above, the response not obtained step would
be entered and the applicant would be directed to isolate the source of the leak (CCW to P-55A
is isolable) and to start additional available primary make pumps to recover level in the surge
tank. With no information regarding the status of isolating the leak or recovering surge tank
level, the applicant would have to make an assumption that CCW inventory was in jeopardy.
Therefore, CCW cooling is maintained to the P-55B and P-55C charging pumps with no
additional information put forth regarding CCW.

The stem of the question did specifically mention that the crew entered and was performing
the actions of AOP-22, Pressurizer Level Control Malfunctions. Step 8, [V]erify charging flow
lowering is the crux of the applicant’s contention. With charging flow lowering as the running
charging pump has tripped, the applicant is asked by the procedure if the charging pumps are
in distress. In distress is defined in the procedure step as making rattling and banging noises
indicative of pumping non-liquid fluids. If the applicant determines the charging pump(s) is/are
in distress they would enter the response not obtained leg of the step which has them isolate
the letdown orifices as the charging pumps need to be vented prior to starting one. Since
venting the charging pumps is a time-consuming process, letdown is isolated in order to prevent
adversely affecting Pressurizer level. The AOP Basis document for AOP-22 specifically


                                                 3
 describes the actions associated with step 8 as addressing a rupture of a charging pump
discharge damper which would gas bind the charging pumps (hence pumping non-liquid fluids).
With nitrogen displacing the water in the charging lines, the charging pumps would need to be
vented prior to restoring charging pump operation. The situation in the stem of the question says
nothing regarding a failure of a charging pump discharge damper nor does it indicate that the
fluid in the leg of piping associated with the charging system is filled with anything but water.

Lastly, when assessing how this question should be adjudicated, it is necessary to consult
NUREG 1021. ES 4.4, C.3.e states in part, that a question cannot have two correct answers
“if both answer choices contain conflicting information.” In this instance Distractor C and
Answer D differ by the fact that one answer says letdown is isolated versus is NOT isolated.
This is based on the assessment that charging is in distress or is NOT in distress. The NUREG
directs that a question which creates the circumstance where two answers which are
diametrically opposed to one another can both be considered correct must be deleted from
the examination. Therefore, even if the analysis indicated that both answers were correct,
accepting both answers would not be a correct response to this applicant’s contention.

NRC Resolution:

Region III evaluated this contention in accordance with NUREG-1021, ES-4.4, paragraph
C.3.c. to determine if the following types of errors were adequately identified and
justified for effecting an answer key change.

   •   Did Question 5 lack necessary information upon which to answer or contain an
       unclear stem that confused the applicants?

       Yes, the applicants’ contention and the facility’s assessment claimed that Question 5
       lacked necessary information upon which to base an answer. One applicant asked a
       question requesting valve component IDs for letdown orifice stop valves during exam
       administration regarding Question 5.

       Region III concluded that Question 5 did not possess an unclear or confusing stem.

   •   Did Question 5 test the wrong license level (RO versus SRO) or was it not linked
       to (SRO) job requirements?

       Neither the applicants’ contention nor facility’s assessment claimed incorrect license
       level or lack of job link as a basis for their respective contentions.

       Region III concluded that Question 5 did not test the wrong license level and that the
       tested subject matter was linked to job requirements. Specifically, (K/A) 000022A
       AK2.07.

   •   Did Question 5 contain unintended typographical errors?

       Neither the applicants’ contention nor facility’s assessment claimed unintended
       typographical errors as a basis for their respective contentions.

       Region III concluded that there were no unintended typographical errors in Question 5.




                                                4
    •   Did either the applicant or facility contention introduce newly discovered technical
       information which supports an answer key change?

       Neither the applicants’ contention nor facility’s assessment claimed newly discovered
       technical information which supports an answer key change.

NRC Recommendation:

In summary, Region III disagrees with the applicant’s contention and in accordance with
NUREG 1021, ES-4.4, paragraph C.3.c, the answer key for the written examination will remain
unchanged with answer choice D as the ONLY correct answer.




                                               5
 Question #26

   •   The Unit is at 100% Power
   •   AOP-33 (FUEL CLADDING FAILURE) actions are in progress
   •   EK-1363 (CONTAINMENT HI RADIATION) is in alarm

___(1)___ in the PCS is an indication of a fuel defect.
Per AOP-33, Letdown is ___(2)___.

             (1)                      (2)
       A. Cesium-137        maintained in service
       B. Cesium-137               isolated
       C. Argon-41          maintained in service
       D. Argon-41                isolated

Answer: B

   A. Incorrect but plausible. Part 1 is correct. For Part 2, maintaining letdown in service
      would be correct if EK-1363 (CONTAINMENT HI RADIATION) was NOT in alarm.
   B. CORRECT. Cs-137 is a fission product. Elevated Cs-137 is indicative of a fuel defect.
      AOP-33 directs the Crew to close the letdown orifice stop valves, isolating letdown
   C. Incorrect but plausible. For Part 1, Ar-41 is not a fission product. It is plausible
      because it is a coolant activation product and is a radio-isotope present in the coolant.
      For Part 2, maintaining letdown in service would be correct if EK-1363 (CONTAINMENT
      HI RADIATION) was not in alarm.
   D. Incorrect but plausible. For Part 1, Ar-41 is not a fission product. It is plausible because
      it is a coolant activation product and is a radio-isotope present in the coolant. Part 2
      is correct.

Question Development:

During examination outline development, Question 26 was selected as Knowledge and Ability
(K/A) 000076AK1.02, to be a Tier 1 question. Questions formulated from this tier are generally
expected to test an applicant’s knowledge of how to safely operate the plant during emergency
and abnormal conditions.

Question 26 was developed by Palisades for use on the 2026 Palisades Initial License Written
Examination. There were no technical or psychometric errors identified by the NRC examination
review team or the Palisades Training Department staff regarding this question during
examination review and facility validation.

Knowledge and Ability (K/A) Statement: Knowledge of the operational implications and/or cause
and effect relationships of the following concepts as they apply to (APE 76) HIGH REACTOR
COOLANT ACTIVITY (CFR: 41.8 / 41.10 / 45.3): Radiation source and/or transport pathway
Rating 3.3




                                                6
 Question Administration:

NUREG-1021, ES-4.3, item B.2.i, identifies that for applicants taking the RO written
examination, six hours is to be allotted.

   •   No applicants asked a question or requested clarification for Question 26 during
       administration of the written examination.
   •   Nine (of fifteen) applicants correctly answered this question. Five applicants selected
       choice A and one applicant selected choice C. (60.0% pass rate).
   •   The question was originally assessed as satisfactory by the NRC Chief Examiner
       during review of the proposed exam.
   •   A post-examination comment proposed an answer key change for Question 26.
       The facility/applicants contesting the question believe there are two correct answers
       for Question 26, answers A and B.

Applicant Comment:

EK-1363 Containment Hi Radiation alarm could be in with one rad monitor and no containment
isolation. Letdown could still be maintained, same as auto action occurred. Per AOP-33 letdown
isn’t automatically maintained / isolated.

Question 26 has two technically correct answers. Palisades’ position is that both answers A and
B are correct.

Facility/Applicant Justification for Comment:

The question stem is ambiguous regarding whether Part 2 is asking for the expected plant
response based on the conditions provided (i.e., an implied automatic action) or the crew’s
manual actions taken during the performance of AOP-33.

A candidate could reasonably interpret the question as asking whether isolation should have
occurred based on the initial conditions in the stem and select the answer corresponding to the
plant's response to the alarm given in the stem. Alarm EK-1363 can annunciate on 1 out of 4
logic for the Containment Area Monitors and is therefore not by itself an indication that letdown
is isolated by the Containment Hi Radiation (CHR) automatic function. The AOP-33 basis
document states, the “intent of the step is to direct performance of actions appropriate for a
Containment Isolation due to a CHR signal.” While the EK-1363 Containment Hi Radiation
alarm is in, the stem of the question does not provide enough information to determine whether
or not a valid CHR signal exists.

Alternatively, a candidate could interpret the question as asking for the actions directed by
AOP-33 and select the answer corresponding to the crew's required procedural response.
In this case, it is reasonable for a candidate to assume that with alarm EK-1363 in during a
fuel cladding failure, a valid CHR signal would exist. However, this could have been ensured
by writing the stem to explicitly state “Per AOP-33, the crew will __(2)__”

As written, the question does not clearly distinguish between automatic system response and
manual operator actions. Therefore, both Answers A and B are supportable and should be
accepted as correct.




                                                7
 Per NUREG 1021, ES 4.4, C.3.c, the question stem was not clear or did not contain all pertinent
information to distinguish between two answer choices.

NRC Assessment:

The question stem explicitly states, “[P]er AOP-33” this indicates the question is asking what
actions are required per the procedure. AOP-33, Fuel Cladding Failure, Step 6 Operator
Actions, Step 2 asks if both EK-1126, “CIS INITIATED” and EK-1363, “CONTAINMENT HI
RADIATION” alarms are clear. The answer to this would be NO as the stem indicates that
EK-1363 is alarming. This would place the operator in the response not obtained column of
step 2 which, in addition to other actions, has them close the Letdown Orifice Stop Valves.

Regarding the applicant’s contention associated with the basis of the step being to,
“direct performance of actions appropriate for a Containment Isolation due to a CHR signal”,
|the Annunciator Response Procedure (ARP) for alarm EK-1363 must be reviewed for expected
operator actions in response to this alarming condition. The ARP corroborates the applicant’s
contention that only one of four channels indicating greater than 10 R/hr will result in
annunciator EK-1363 alarming and that 2 of 4 channels must be greater than 10 R/hr to
result in a containment isolation signal based on high radiation or a CHR. The ARP also
instructs the crew to verify that a containment isolation signal has been generated if actual
containment radiation is greater than 10 R/hr on any single {emphasis added} Containment
Area Monitor and if it hasn’t, manually actuate one by pushing the left or right High Radiation
Initiate Pushbutton. The stem of the question provides no information that would indicate that a
failed channel has occurred. The applicant would have to be making an assumption regarding
the signal being invalid. In addition, there is no information as to whether it’s one or possibly
more channels which have exceeded the 10 R/hr setpoint. Again, the applicant would be
making an assumption of the number of channels exceeding the alarm setpoint. If it is more
than one channel, than the CHR would have occurred automatically and if it is only one channel
than the ARP directs a manual actuation of CHR. Regardless of the number of alarming
channels, AOP-33 directs manually isolating the Letdown Orifice Isolation Valves because
EK-1363 is alarming.

Lastly, when assessing how this question should be adjudicated, it is necessary to consult
NUREG 1021. ES 4.4, C.3.e states in part, that a question cannot have two correct answers
“if both answer choices contain conflicting information.” In this instance Distractor A and
Answer B differ by the fact that one answer says letdown is isolated versus is NOT isolated.

The basis for both answers is that the concerns of thermal shock and water hammer are
intrinsically linked under the conditions presented. Slowly opening the valve minimizes rapid
temperature changes, reducing the potential for thermal shock. Additionally, slowly admitting
steam helps prevent steam collapse and condensate acceleration, which are precursors to
water hammer.

SOP-10 requires slow and controlled system heating and restoration for both thermal shock
(page 10/11) and water hammer (page 61). On page 10, Heater Drain Pump warming is
performed to prevent rapid temperature changes creating thermal stresses and pump damage.
Similarly, page 61 requires slow and controlled system restoration when opening the T-4A,
Reheater Drain Tank, normal drain lines to E-6A, High Pressure Feedwater Heater, specifically
calling out water hammer damage to MSRs, control valves or drain tank piping.

The same operator action (slow and controlled system heating and restoration) addresses both
thermal shock and water hammer concerns. A candidate could reasonably select either answer.
The question does not establish a clear distinction that would make one consequence more
correct than the other. Therefore, both Answers A and C are technically supportable and should
be accepted as correct.

NRC Assessment:

Answer choice A is clearly a correct answer and is specifically mentioned as a reason for
controlled operation when introducing steam into feedwater heater piping when performing
SOP-10, Extraction and Heater Drain System. Thermal shock can also be a challenge to piping
when a significant differential temperature exists across the wall of a pipe. A differential
temperature of 100oC between the inner and outer wall of a carbon steel pipe would generate
approximately 36 kpsi of thermal stress on the piping (Callen, Thermal Shock in Carbon Steel
Pipe: Temperature Differential Limits, April 5, 2026). In addition, repeated rapid introduction of
steam or high temperature fluid into cold piping can create small flaws which through fatigue
growth over numerous iterations could result in failure of the impacted carbon steel piping.

 NRC Assessment:

Five applicants requested a reference to answer this question based on a greater than 1 hour
required action time being assessed. No reference was provided to the applicants during
the examination. Per NUREG 1021, a 1 hour required action time is the distinguishing feature
between RO and SRO level of knowledge. RO’s are expected to recall TS action statements
and safety limits which must be addressed in 1 hour. SRO’s are expected to recall TS action
statements and safety limits which are > 1 hour. Since this question appeared on the
SRO-ONLY portion of the written examination it did not require the applicants to recall from
memory information that would be beyond what they were expected to know, it was appropriate
that no reference was provided. In this instance, not providing a reference had no adverse
impact on the applicants’ ability to answer the question as all applicants selected Distractor C
which correctly answered how long the crew had to lower power < 75% to address the
misaligned control rods.

The applicant’s contention is associated with part 2 of the question. Specifically, the implications
for operating with misaligned control rods if mitigating action steps are not taken in a timely
manner. The question stem indicates that the reactor is operating at 100% power. The stem
makes no mention of any planned rod movements or power changes. The stem then indicates
that rod position deviation alarms have come in. Without making any assumptions, this would
indicate and a reasonable diagnosis can be made that at least one control rod has partially
or fully dropped into the core as no operator action had taken place to move control rods.
The TS 3.1.4, Control Rod Alignment basis document specifically discusses the implications
of a rod misalignment caused by a dropped control rod:

      The third type of mis-operation occurs when one rod drops partially or fully into the
      reactor core. This event causes an initial power reduction followed by a return towards
      the original power, due to positive reactivity feedback from the negative moderator
      temperature coefficient. Increased peaking during the power increase may result in
      excessive local Linear Heat Rates (LHRs) {emphasis added}.

The TS actions are designed to ensure the assumptions in the safety analysis remain valid.
In this case, lowering power will move the reactor away from thermal limits. Correct Answer D
is also justified by the TS 3.1.4 basis document where it states:

      If one control rod is misaligned by > 8 inches continued operation in MODES 1 and 2 may
      continue, provided, within 2 hours, the TOTAL RADIAL PEAKING FACTOR has been
      verified acceptable in accordance with SR 3.2.2.1, or the power is reduced to  75% RTP.

      Xenon redistribution in the core starts to occur as soon as a rod becomes misaligned
      {emphasis added}. Reducing THERMAL POWER to  75% RTP ensures acceptable
      power distributions are maintained.
